result.description: Kaia's Island Kitchen & Tiki Bar opened in April 2025 at 480 Hartz Ave in downtown Danville, in the space that was formerly The Vine and Spirits wine bar. Veteran Danville restaurateur Randy Negi (longtime owner of Bridges and a partner at Danville Brewing Company) built the concept around family trips to Hawaii and named it for his granddaughter Kaia, whose painted portrait greets guests near the entrance. The menu is food-first Hawaiian comfort fare — Spam musubi, poke crisps and bowls, loco moco, chicken katsu, kalbi beef, macadamia-crusted catch and a shareable Hula Pie — paired with a serious tiki program (a '44 Mai Tai, Ohanapod Mai Tai, Chi Chi, Zombie, Navy Grog, rum flights) assembled with help from Danville Brewing head brewer Matt Sager. The room mixes bamboo, thatch, carved tiki statues, blown-glass orbs, a sunset beach mural and colorful lighting, with an island garden patio (heaters and tiki torches), a reservable "Celi's Beach Hut," daily brunch and lunch, a keiki menu, and live Hawaiian music on Fridays.

result.description: Rancho Cantina Danville is the second location of the family-owned Lafayette original, opened by longtime Danville residents Nico and Alice Tzikas in the former Cocina Hermanas building on the corner of Hartz Avenue and Church Street. The kitchen, led by Executive Chef Carlos Navarro, cooks over a wood-fired (almond wood) grill and describes its food as inspired by the Spanish-Mexican Californios of California's ranching era: Vaquero Platters, carne asada, brick chicken, a 32 oz Cowboy Cut ribeye, and whole fried branzino alongside tacos, enchiladas, burritos and sizzling fajita skillets. The larger Danville building allowed a more substantial bar built around tequila and mezcal cocktails and a five-margarita lineup, with outdoor seating on the Hartz Avenue corner. It soft-opened Monday, August 24, 2026, with full online reservations from September 1.

result.description: Danville Harvest is a farm-to-table restaurant in downtown Danville led by Executive Chef Noe Briseno, built around sustainably sourced, seasonal Bay Area ingredients with an approachable menu of shared small plates, salads and mains. It describes itself as "a pillar of the downtown community," serving weekday lunch, weekend brunch, daily dinner and a daily happy hour. Its bar program bills itself as award-winning, with seasonal craft cocktails, a "Build your own Manhattan" project and what it calls the largest whiskey selection in the Tri-Valley. The restaurant is part of restaurateur Darren Matte's group, which also runs Cocina Hermanas (Danville), Parkside Los Gatos and Per Diem (San Francisco).

result.walking_notes: All four sit within about 250 ft of each other around the Hartz Ave & Church St intersection (OSM intersection node 37.820604, -121.998233). Hartz Ave runs NW–SE through downtown; odd numbers (Incontro 455, Rancho 501) are on the southwest side, even numbers (Kaia's 480, Harvest 500) on the northeast side. Church St crosses Hartz here (running SW to Railroad Ave and NE toward Front St / Bridges). Layout by quadrant: Rancho Cantina occupies the corner building south of Church on the SW side (DanvilleSanRamon: 'southeast corner of Hartz Avenue and Church Street'); Danville Harvest is directly across Hartz from Rancho, south of Church on the NE side (about 120 ft / one crosswalk apart); Kaia's is on Harvest's side of Hartz, roughly 110 ft northwest of the intersection (across Church St from Harvest, ~160 ft door to door); Incontro is on Rancho's side, about 170 ft northwest of the intersection (across Church St from Rancho, ~220 ft; 485 Hartz/New Moon Massage sits between Incontro and the corner). Pairwise distances (building centroids): Rancho–Harvest ~120 ft, Kaia's–Harvest ~160 ft, Incontro–Kaia's ~155 ft, Rancho–Kaia's ~215 ft, Rancho–Incontro ~220 ft, Incontro–Harvest ~250 ft — every pairing is under a one-minute walk with at most one street crossing. The Hartz/Church intersection was the first phase (April 2024) of the Town's $4.9M Downtown Master Plan Catalyst Project, which added enhanced pedestrian crossings, traffic-calming bulb-outs and new lighting at five Hartz intersections from School St to Linda Mesa Ave, so the crossing between Rancho and Harvest is a rebuilt pedestrian crossing. Church St and School St are 2-hour street parking; Hartz Ave is mostly 2-hour with loading zones (Town parking map). Nearest lots: Village Theatre Municipal Lot ~340 ft NE via Church St; Front Street Municipal Lot ~420 ft; Railroad Ave Municipal Lot ~440 ft SW via Church St (backs onto the Iron Horse Trail, which passes ~40 ft from Railroad & Church). Upscale neighbors inside the same pocket: Bridges Restaurant & Bar at 44 Church St (~230 ft NE of the corner) and Crush'd Wine Bar + Kitchen at 312 Railroad Ave (~210 ft SW).
result.neighborhood_description: The four restaurants anchor the quieter southern end of Danville's historic Hartz Avenue, one block north of where Hartz meets San Ramon Valley Blvd/Hartz Way and a two-to-three-minute walk south of the busier Prospect Ave/Danville Hotel/Prospect Park Plaza core. This stretch is where Danville's late-1800s/early-1900s residences were converted into restaurants: Incontro occupies the c.1910 Hartz House (home of John Hartz, the subdivider who created Hartz Avenue), Harvest the c.1903 Eddy House, and further south sit the Cabral House (551), Bret Read House (571) and Shuey/Podva House (100 School St) from the Town's Historic Downtown Walking Tour. Bay Area Telegraph calls the Hartz/Church corner 'one of downtown Danville's busiest restaurant stretches'; the Town's Catalyst Project (2024–25) rebuilt the intersection with bulb-outs, enhanced crossings and new light poles/lit bollards. Within ~250 ft are Bridges Restaurant & Bar (44 Church St, the Mrs. Doubtfire restaurant) and Crush'd Wine Bar + Kitchen (312 Railroad Ave, 24 wines on tap); the Village Theatre & Art Gallery (233 Front St, the 1874 Grange Hall) is ~315 ft NE; the Iron Horse Trail and the Railroad Ave lot (Saturday Farmers' Market) are one short block SW via Church St. The Town's official 'Live Locally' branding, the oak-tree logo and the 350-year-old Old Oak Tree (Diablo Rd, ~980 ft NE) frame the local identity. Compared with the north-Hartz/Prospect block (dive bar, music club, piano bar, brewery), this pocket is dinner-and-patio oriented: wood-fired Californio Mexican (Rancho, opened Aug 24, 2026), regional Italian in a historic house (Incontro, closed Mondays), farm-to-table (Harvest, dinner ends 8:30 pm daily) and Hawaiian/tiki cocktails with live Hawaiian music (Kaia's, bar to 11 pm Fri–Sat). Hours as read Sept 10, 2026 — Rancho Sun–Thu 11–10, Fri–Sat 11–11; Incontro dinner Tue–Thu & Sun 5–9, Fri–Sat 5–10, brunch buffet Sat 12–3 / Sun 10–2; Kaia's Sun–Tue 11:30–9, Wed–Thu 11:30–10, Fri–Sat 11:30–11 (kitchen closes an hour before the bar); Harvest lunch weekdays 11:30–3, brunch weekends 10–3, dinner daily 4–8:30, happy hour 3–5.

result.town_facts: Town of Danville, Contra Costa County (East Bay), 'Heart of the San Ramon Valley'; ~30 miles east of San Francisco. Population 43,582 (2020 Census, Wikipedia) / 'approximately 43,146' (Town Community Profile); 18 sq mi; incorporated July 1, 1982 and one of the few California municipalities styled 'Town'. Founded 1854 by brothers Daniel and Andrew Inman on 400 acres bought with Gold Rush earnings; named Danville by 1858; post office 1860. The Southern Pacific branch line arrived June 7, 1891; John Hartz gave/sold 8.65 acres for the depot and subdivided 74 lots east of it, shifting commerce from Front St to the new Hartz Avenue; the Danville Hotel was turned to face Hartz in 1927. Wealthy, family-oriented suburb: Wikipedia cites ZIP 94506 as the 14th-wealthiest in America and the town as 2nd-highest-income U.S. place with 40,000+ residents. SafeWise named Danville California's safest city for 2026 (No. 1 six of the past nine years; violent crime 0.6 and property crime 5.9 per 1,000) — Town news release Feb 12, 2026. Town copy describes 'the perfect blend of upscale amenities and small-town charm', a 'quaint character', highly rated schools, year-round farmers' markets and street fairs, and a historic downtown of shops, restaurants and galleries 'from upscale eateries to family-friendly pizzerias'. Official brand since 2017: 'Live Locally' with an oak-tree logo (#LiveLocallyDanville); the 350-year-old Old Oak Tree on Diablo Rd is the town symbol and mascot Auggie the Acorn's home. Downtown investment: $4.9M Downtown Master Plan Catalyst Project (begun April 2024 at Hartz & Church) rebuilt five Hartz intersections from School St to Linda Mesa with raised/bulb-out crossings, lit bollards and new light poles; Prospect Park Plaza reopened July 2025 with a stage and oak sculptures; a new Town Green Pavilion starts construction Aug 2026 (done Spring 2027). What closes early (as read Sept 10, 2026): Museum of the SRV by 4 pm; Danville Harvest dinner ends 8:30 pm daily; Bridges dinner ends 8 pm Sun–Thu / 9 pm Fri–Sat; Danville Brewing bar 9 pm (9:30 Fri–Sat); Incontro 9 pm Tue–Thu & Sun, 10 pm Fri–Sat (closed Mondays); Crush'd 9 pm (10 Thu–Sat); Kaia's 9 pm Sun–Tue, 10 Wed–Thu, 11 Fri–Sat; Rancho Cantina 10 pm (11 Fri–Sat); Revel and Norm's 10–11 pm; Auburn Lounge is the late option at midnight nightly. The two 1-am venues (Kick N Mule, Stilettos) are listed closed. Farmers' Market Saturdays 9–1; Town offices M–Th 8–5, F 8–1. Downtown parking is free (1,400+ public spaces, six municipal lots), which the Town and press consistently highlight.

Lot capacities are not published except OSM's 82 for the Library lot. Sycamore Valley Park & Ride was not geocoded.
